g: Vocative + ustedes command
‘Hijos’ directly addresses children, and obedezcan is the ustedes imperative. Personal a introduces the people obeyed, sus padres.
e: en el Señor
This compact prepositional phrase frames the command within relationship to the Lord; it modifies obedezcan, not padres.

g: Quoted tú command with parenthesis
‘Honra’ addresses one person in the singular. The em-dash opens Paul's explanatory parenthesis, whose subject is the preceding commandment.
e: el primer mandamiento con promesa
Con promesa means ‘with a promise attached.’ Primer is the shortened masculine singular form used before mandamiento.

v: it may go well with you
g: Para que + two subjunctives
‘Para que te vaya bien y disfrutes’ gives the promised result with subjunctive vaya and disfrutes; te marks the singular person addressed.
e: una larga vida en la tierra
Larga precedes vida naturally and describes duration. En la tierra can mean ‘on the earth’ or ‘in the land’ in this quoted promise.

g: No ... sino ... between commands
‘No hagan enojar’ uses hacer + infinitive as a negative command; sino replaces it with affirmative críenlos, whose los refers to hijos.
e: la disciplina e instrucción del Señor
E replaces y before instrucción because the next word begins with the /i/ sound; both nouns describe the manner of raising the children.

g: Vocative + command with con phrases
‘Esclavos’ addresses the group; obedezcan takes personal a, while con respeto y temor and con integridad describe manner.
e: como a Cristo
Como introduces the standard of service, ‘as [you would obey] Christ.’ The preposition a is retained from obedecer a.

v: to win or earn for oneself
g: No solo cuando + subjunctive
‘No lo hagan solo cuando los estén mirando’ rejects conduct limited to occasions of being watched; estén mirando is subjunctive in that restricted setting.
e: ganarse el favor humano
Ganarse el favor de alguien means ‘to win someone's favor.’ The reflexive pronoun gives the sense of securing the benefit for oneself.

g: Como quien + present indicative
‘Como quien sirve al Señor’ means ‘as one who serves the Lord.’ Quien is singular and generic, so sirve appears in third-person singular.
e: al Señor y no a los hombres
The parallel personal objects contrast the true orientation of service: al contracts a + el, while a is repeated before los hombres.

g: El bien que + perfect subjunctive
‘El bien que haya hecho’ uses perfect subjunctive for whatever good each person may have done; future recompensará gives the result.
e: sea esclavo o sea libre
Repeated subjunctive sea presents an exhaustive alternative, ‘whether slave or free,’ showing that cada uno includes either status.

g: Commands plus a gerund of cessation
‘Correspondan’ and ‘recuerden’ address masters directly; dejando de amenazarlos means ‘stopping threatening them’ and supplies the required change.
e: tanto ellos como ustedes tienen un mismo Amo
Tanto ... como means ‘both ... and.’ Amo is capitalized here as a title for the one heavenly Master shared by both groups.

g: Pronominal command + con of means
‘Fortalézcanse con’ commands the plural audience to draw strength by means of the Lord's power; se attaches to the affirmative imperative.
e: el gran poder del Señor
Gran is the shortened form of grande before a singular noun. Del contracts de + el and identifies the source of the power.

g: Para que + poder in the subjunctive
‘Para que puedan hacer frente’ states purpose, so poder appears as subjunctive puedan before the fixed verbal phrase hacer frente.
e: hacer frente a las artimañas
Hacer frente a means ‘to stand against’ or ‘confront.’ The a is part of the expression, not the personal a.

g: No es contra ... sino contra ...
The sentence denies one opponent category and replaces it with a four-part series; repeated contra keeps each category parallel.
e: fuerzas espirituales malignas
Both espirituales and malignas agree with feminine plural fuerzas; the phrase names the final category in the repeated contra series.

g: Future time clause + purpose subjunctive
‘Cuando llegue el día malo’ uses subjunctive for a future event, and ‘para que ... puedan’ adds the purpose of putting on the armor.
e: hasta el fin con firmeza
Hasta el fin marks endurance to the endpoint; con firmeza describes the steadfast manner of remaining after resistance.

g: Command followed by plural participles
‘Manténganse firmes’ is the main command; ceñidos and protegidos agree with the plural audience and describe their equipped state.
e: el cinturón de la verdad
Cinturón is the belt in the armor image. De la verdad identifies truth with the equipment around which ceñidos is constructed.

g: Participial continuation without a finite verb
‘Y calzados’ continues the equipped-state descriptions from verse 14. The understood subject remains the plural recipients.
e: el evangelio de la paz
De la paz specifies the content or character of evangelio, ‘the gospel of peace,’ within the image of readiness as footwear.

g: Con el cual + poder + infinitive
‘Con el cual pueden apagar’ uses the relative el cual to refer unambiguously to masculine escudo; pueden governs infinitive apagar.
e: Además de todo esto
Además de means ‘in addition to’ or, in context, ‘besides/above all this.’ The phrase links the shield to the preceding equipment.

g: Que es identifies the metaphor
‘La espada del Espíritu, que es la palabra de Dios’ uses a relative clause to identify what the sword represents; que refers to espada.
e: la palabra de Dios
Palabra means ‘word’ or ‘message.’ Here the relative clause directly equates it with the Spirit's sword in the armor image.

g: Series of ustedes commands
‘Oren,’ ‘manténganse,’ and ‘perseveren’ are coordinated plural commands; con phrases specify kinds of prayer and alertness.
e: en todo momento
This time expression means ‘at all times.’ Singular momento follows todo and gives the scope of oren.

g: Para que + subjunctive, with embedded cuando
‘Para que ... Dios me dé’ states the purpose of prayer; subjunctive hable follows cuando because each future occasion of speaking is anticipated.
e: dar a conocer con valor el misterio del evangelio
Dar a conocer means ‘to make known.’ Con valor describes the bold manner, and del evangelio specifies the mystery's relation to the gospel.

g: Por el cual as a relative link
‘Por el cual soy embajador’ refers back to el evangelio; para que lo proclame then uses subjunctive to state the requested outcome.
e: embajador en cadenas
The phrase places an official representative ‘in chains,’ a striking description of Paul's commissioned role while imprisoned.

g: Apposition followed by a purpose clause
‘Nuestro querido hermano Tíquico, fiel servidor’ uses two appositive descriptions; ‘para que ... sepan’ takes subjunctive after purpose.
e: cómo me va y qué estoy haciendo
Cómo and qué carry accents because they introduce indirect questions: how things are going for Paul and what he is doing.

g: Para que + two coordinated subjunctives
‘Para que sepan ... y para que cobren’ repeats the purpose conjunction; sepan and cobren give the two intended results of envío.
e: cobren ánimo
Cobrar ánimo is an idiom meaning ‘take courage’ or ‘be encouraged’; cobrar here means acquire, not charge money.

g: Que + plural subjunctive for a blessing
‘Que Dios el Padre y el Señor Jesucristo les concedan’ expresses a wish; concedan is plural because two coordinated subjects grant the gifts.
e: paz, amor y fe a los hermanos
Three coordinated nouns are the direct objects of concedan, while a los hermanos names those who receive them.

g: Sea for a closing wish
‘La gracia sea con todos’ uses present subjunctive sea as a benediction. The relative los que aman identifies the recipients.
e: con amor imperecedero
Imperecedero means ‘undying’ or ‘incorruptible’ and agrees with masculine amor, characterizing the love named in this closing line.
